imc-2000-01.title: Supremum argument for (a), explicit counterexample for (b)
imc-2000-01.body:
**a) Yes.** Let $f$ be increasing (non-decreasing) and put
$$A=\{x\in[0,1]:\ f(x)\ge x\}.$$
Since $f(0)\ge 0$, we have $0\in A$, so $A$ is non-empty and bounded; let $a=\sup A\in[0,1]$.

* For every $x\in A$ we have $x\le a$, hence $x\le f(x)\le f(a)$. So $f(a)$ is an upper bound of $A$, and therefore $a\le f(a)$.
* Applying $f$ to $a\le f(a)$ gives $f(a)\le f(f(a))$, i.e. the point $f(a)\in[0,1]$ belongs to $A$. Hence $f(a)\le \sup A=a$.

Together, $f(a)=a$: the point $a$ is a fixed point. (Continuity is not needed.)

**b) No.** Define
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}1-\dfrac x2, & 0\le x\le \tfrac12,\\[2mm] \dfrac12-\dfrac x2, & \tfrac12<x\le 1.\end{cases}$$
On $[0,\tfrac12]$ the values lie in $[\tfrac34,1]$, on $(\tfrac12,1]$ they lie in $[0,\tfrac14)$; so $f$ maps $[0,1]$ into $[0,1]$, it is decreasing on each piece, and it jumps down at $\tfrac12$, so it is decreasing on $[0,1]$.

There is no fixed point: for $x\le\tfrac12$ we have $f(x)\ge\tfrac34>x$, and for $x>\tfrac12$ we have $f(x)<\tfrac14<x$.

**Answer: a) Yes; b) No.** ∎

imc-2000-02.title: Divide by $w-z$ and use symmetric functions
imc-2000-02.body:
Since $w\ne z$ we may divide the differences by $w-z$. Write
$$h(w,z)=\frac{w^5-z^5}{w-z}=w^4+w^3z+w^2z^2+wz^3+z^4 .$$
Then
$$\frac{p(w)-p(z)}{w-z}=h(w,z)+1,\qquad \frac{q(w)-q(z)}{w-z}=h(w,z)+(w+z).$$
So the conditions are equivalent to
$$h(w,z)+1=0\quad\text{and}\quad h(w,z)+w+z=0 .$$
Subtracting gives $w+z=1$.

Let $s=w+z$ and $c=wz$. Express $h$ through $s,c$:
$$w^4+z^4=(s^2-2c)^2-2c^2,\qquad w^3z+wz^3=c(s^2-2c),\qquad w^2z^2=c^2,$$
so $h=s^4-3s^2c+c^2$. With $s=1$ the condition $h=-1$ becomes
$$1-3c+c^2=-1\iff c^2-3c+2=0\iff c\in\{1,2\}.$$

* $c=1$: $w,z$ are the roots of $t^2-t+1=0$, i.e. $\frac{1\pm\sqrt3\,i}{2}$.
* $c=2$: $w,z$ are the roots of $t^2-t+2=0$, i.e. $\frac{1\pm\sqrt7\,i}{2}$.

In both cases the two roots are distinct, so $w\ne z$. Conversely, every such pair has $w+z=1$ and $h(w,z)=-1$, so both divided differences vanish, i.e. $p(w)=p(z)$ and $q(w)=q(z)$.

**Answer:** $(w,z)=\left(\frac{1+\sqrt3 i}{2},\frac{1-\sqrt3 i}{2}\right)$, $\left(\frac{1-\sqrt3 i}{2},\frac{1+\sqrt3 i}{2}\right)$, $\left(\frac{1+\sqrt7 i}{2},\frac{1-\sqrt7 i}{2}\right)$, $\left(\frac{1-\sqrt7 i}{2},\frac{1+\sqrt7 i}{2}\right)$. ∎

imc-2000-03.title: Write the rank-one matrix as $uv^T$
imc-2000-03.body:
Let $C=AB-BA$. A matrix of rank $1$ can be written as $C=uv^{T}$ with non-zero column vectors $u,v\in\mathbb C^n$ (all columns of $C$ are multiples of one non-zero column $u$; collect the multipliers in $v$).

Then
$$C^2=u\,(v^{T}u)\,v^{T}=(v^{T}u)\,C .$$
The scalar $v^Tu=\sum_i u_iv_i$ is exactly the trace of $uv^T=C$. But
$$\operatorname{tr}C=\operatorname{tr}(AB)-\operatorname{tr}(BA)=0 ,$$
since $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$ for all square matrices. Hence $C^2=0\cdot C=0$. ∎

imc-2000-03.title: Eigenvalues and Jordan form
imc-2000-03.body:
Again let $C=AB-BA$. Since $\operatorname{rank}C=1$, the kernel of $C$ has dimension $n-1$, so $0$ is an eigenvalue of geometric (hence also algebraic) multiplicity at least $n-1$. The remaining eigenvalue $\lambda$ satisfies $\lambda=\operatorname{tr}C=0$. So all eigenvalues of $C$ are $0$ and $C$ is nilpotent.

In the Jordan normal form of $C$ the number of Jordan blocks equals $\dim\ker C=n-1$, so there are $n-1$ blocks of total size $n$: one block of size $2$ and $n-2$ blocks of size $1$. The square of a nilpotent Jordan block of size at most $2$ is zero, so $C^2=0$. ∎

imc-2000-04.title: Expand the square; then swap the order of summation
imc-2000-04.body:
**a)** All terms are positive, so
$$\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{x_i}{\sqrt i}\right)^2=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{x_i}{\sqrt i}\frac{x_j}{\sqrt j}\ \ge\ \sum_{i=1}^n\frac{x_i}{\sqrt i}\sum_{j=1}^{i}\frac{x_j}{\sqrt j},$$
where we dropped the terms with $j>i$. For $j\le i$ we have $x_j\ge x_i$ and $\frac1{\sqrt j}\ge\frac1{\sqrt i}$, so $\sum_{j=1}^i\frac{x_j}{\sqrt j}\ge i\cdot\frac{x_i}{\sqrt i}=\sqrt i\,x_i$. Therefore
$$\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{x_i}{\sqrt i}\right)^2\ge\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{x_i}{\sqrt i}\cdot\sqrt i\,x_i=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 ,$$
and taking square roots gives (a).

**b)** We may assume $\sum x_i<\infty$ (otherwise there is nothing to prove). Fix $m$. The tail $x_m,x_{m+1},\dots$ is again decreasing and positive, so by (a) for every $N\ge m$
$$\left(\sum_{i=m}^N x_i^2\right)^{1/2}\le\sum_{i=m}^N\frac{x_i}{\sqrt{i-m+1}}\le\sum_{i=m}^\infty\frac{x_i}{\sqrt{i-m+1}} ;$$
letting $N\to\infty$, the same bound holds for the infinite tail. Summing over $m$ and exchanging the order of summation (all terms are non-negative):
$$\sum_{m=1}^\infty\frac1{\sqrt m}\left(\sum_{i=m}^\infty x_i^2\right)^{1/2}\le\sum_{m=1}^\infty\sum_{i=m}^\infty\frac{x_i}{\sqrt m\sqrt{i-m+1}}=\sum_{i=1}^\infty x_i\,S_i,\qquad S_i=\sum_{m=1}^{i}\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}\sqrt{i+1-m}} .$$
It remains to bound $S_i$ by a constant. The summand is symmetric under $m\leftrightarrow i+1-m$, and for $m\le\frac{i+1}2$ we have $i+1-m\ge\frac{i+1}2$. Hence, with $K=\lfloor\frac{i+1}2\rfloor$,
$$S_i\le 2\sum_{m=1}^{K}\frac{1}{\sqrt m\,\sqrt{(i+1)/2}}\le\frac{2}{\sqrt{(i+1)/2}}\cdot2\sqrt K\le 4,$$
using $\sum_{m=1}^K\frac1{\sqrt m}\le\sum_{m=1}^K 2(\sqrt m-\sqrt{m-1})=2\sqrt K$ (because $\frac1{\sqrt m}\le\frac{2}{\sqrt m+\sqrt{m-1}}$) and $K\le\frac{i+1}2$. (The factor 2 may count a middle term twice; that only makes the bound larger.)

Thus the inequality holds with $C=4$. ∎

imc-2000-04.title: A sharper constant from an integral
imc-2000-04.body:
Part (a) and the reduction of (b) to bounding $S_i=\sum_{m=1}^{i}\frac{1}{\sqrt{m(i+1-m)}}$ are as in the first solution.

The function $h(x)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x(i+1-x)}}$ is convex on $(0,i+1)$ (its logarithm $-\frac12\ln x-\frac12\ln(i+1-x)$ is convex, and the exponential of a convex function is convex). For a convex function the value at the midpoint of an interval is at most the average over the interval, so
$$h(m)\le\int_{m-1/2}^{m+1/2}h(x)\,dx\qquad(1\le m\le i).$$
Summing,
$$S_i\le\int_{1/2}^{i+1/2}h(x)\,dx<\int_0^{i+1}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x(i+1-x)}}=\pi ,$$
where the last integral is computed with $x=(i+1)\sin^2\theta$, $dx=2(i+1)\sin\theta\cos\theta\,d\theta$, giving $\int_0^{\pi/2}2\,d\theta=\pi$.

So the inequality in (b) holds with $C=\pi$. ∎

imc-2000-05.title: Square $g=-(e+f)$ and commute with $e$
imc-2000-05.body:
Throughout we use: if $na=0$ for a positive integer $n$, then $a=0$.

**Step 1.** Since $g=-(e+f)$,
$$g=g^2=(e+f)^2=e^2+ef+fe+f^2=e+f+ef+fe=-g+ef+fe ,$$
so
$$ef+fe=2g. \tag{1}$$

**Step 2: $e$ and $f$ commute.** Multiply (1) by $e$ on the left and on the right:
$$ef+efe=2eg,\qquad efe+fe=2ge .$$
Subtracting, $ef-fe=2(eg-ge)$. Now $eg=e(-e-f)=-e-ef$ and $ge=-e-fe$, so $eg-ge=-(ef-fe)$. Hence $ef-fe=-2(ef-fe)$, i.e. $3(ef-fe)=0$, and therefore $ef=fe$.

**Step 3.** Now (1) reads $2ef=2g$, so $ef=g$ and the hypothesis becomes
$$e+f+ef=0. \tag{2}$$
Multiplying (2) by $e$ on the left gives $e+ef+ef=0$, i.e. $e=-2ef$; multiplying by $f$ on the left gives $fe+f+fef=ef+f+ef=0$ (using $fe=ef$, $f^2=f$), i.e. $f=-2ef$. Thus $e=f$.

**Step 4.** With $f=e$: $e=-2ef=-2e^2=-2e$, so $3e=0$ and $e=0$. Then $f=e=0$ and $g=-(e+f)=0$. ∎

imc-2000-06.title: Compare $F(a_n)$ with $n$ via the mean value theorem
imc-2000-06.body:
**Preliminaries.** $F'=f>0$, so $F$ is continuous and strictly increasing; $F(0)=0$ and $F(x)\ge f(0)x\to\infty$, so $b_n=F^{-1}(n)$ is well defined for $n\ge0$, and $b_n\to\infty$ (as $F$ is bounded on bounded sets). Let $B$ be a bound for $f'$, so $f(u)-f(v)\le B(u-v)$ for $u\ge v$.

The sequence $(a_n)$ is increasing. It is unbounded: otherwise $a_n\to L$ and $a_{n+1}-a_n=1/f(a_n)\ge1/f(L)>0$, impossible. Hence $a_n\to\infty$ and $f(a_n)\to\infty$.

**Step 1.** By the mean value theorem there is $\xi_k\in(a_k,a_{k+1})$ with
$$F(a_{k+1})-F(a_k)=f(\xi_k)(a_{k+1}-a_k)=\frac{f(\xi_k)}{f(a_k)} .$$
Since $f$ is increasing, $f(a_k)\le f(\xi_k)\le f(a_{k+1})$, so
$$F(a_{k+1})-F(a_k)=1+d_k,\qquad 0\le d_k\le\frac{f(a_{k+1})-f(a_k)}{f(a_k)} .$$
Summing over $k=0,\dots,n-1$ and using $F(b_n)=n$:
$$F(a_n)-F(b_n)=F(1)+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}d_k. \tag{1}$$
As $F(1)>0$ and $d_k\ge0$, we get $F(a_n)>F(b_n)$, hence $a_n>b_n$.

**Step 2: the right side of (1) is $o(f(a_n))$.** Let $\varepsilon>0$ and choose $K$ with $f(a_K)>2/\varepsilon$. For $n>K$,
$$\sum_{k=K}^{n-1}d_k\le\frac{1}{f(a_K)}\sum_{k=K}^{n-1}\bigl(f(a_{k+1})-f(a_k)\bigr)<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}f(a_n).$$
The remaining part $F(1)+\sum_{k<K}d_k$ is a constant, which is $<\frac\varepsilon2 f(a_n)$ for large $n$ because $f(a_n)\to\infty$. Hence for all large $n$
$$F(a_n)-F(b_n)<\varepsilon f(a_n). \tag{2}$$

**Step 3: back to $a_n-b_n$.** By the mean value theorem, $F(a_n)-F(b_n)=f(\zeta)(a_n-b_n)$ for some $\zeta\in(b_n,a_n)$, and $f(\zeta)\ge f(b_n)$. Also $f(a_n)\le f(b_n)+B(a_n-b_n)$. Inserting into (2):
$$f(b_n)(a_n-b_n)<\varepsilon f(b_n)+\varepsilon B(a_n-b_n),\quad\text{i.e.}\quad \bigl(f(b_n)-\varepsilon B\bigr)(a_n-b_n)<\varepsilon f(b_n).$$
Since $b_n\to\infty$, $f(b_n)\to\infty$, so for large $n$ we have $f(b_n)>2\varepsilon B$ and therefore
$$0<a_n-b_n<\frac{\varepsilon f(b_n)}{f(b_n)-\varepsilon B}<2\varepsilon .$$
As $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary, $a_n-b_n\to0$. ∎

imc-2000-07.title: Refinements plus a Frobenius-coin lemma
imc-2000-07.body:
Part (a) is the case $d=2$ of (b), so we prove (b) for any $d\ge2$.

**Lemma.** If $a,b$ are coprime positive integers, then every integer $m\ge a(b-1)$ can be written as $m=ax+by$ with integers $x,y\ge0$.

*Proof.* The numbers $0,a,2a,\dots,(b-1)a$ are pairwise incongruent modulo $b$ (as $\gcd(a,b)=1$), so they form a complete residue system; choose $x\in\{0,\dots,b-1\}$ with $ax\equiv m\pmod b$. Then $m-ax\ge m-a(b-1)\ge0$ is divisible by $b$, and $y=(m-ax)/b\ge0$ works. $\square$

**Refinement.** Given a dissection of the cube into $k$ cubes, pick any one of them and cut it into $a^d$ equal cubes (divide each of its edges into $a$ equal parts). This gives a dissection into $k+(a^d-1)$ cubes. Starting from the unit cube itself ($k=1$) and refining repeatedly (each time some cube of the current dissection), we can reach
$$1+x(a_1^d-1)+y(a_2^d-1)\qquad\text{pieces, for all }x,y\ge0,$$
for any fixed $a_1,a_2\ge2$.

**Coprime increments.** Take $a_1=2$ and $a_2=2^d-1$ (which is $\ge3$ for $d\ge2$). Put $P=2^d-1$ and $R=(2^d-1)^d-1=P^d-1$. A common divisor of $P$ and $R$ divides $P^d$ and $P^d-1$, hence divides $1$; so $\gcd(P,R)=1$.

By the lemma every $m\ge P(R-1)$ is of the form $xP+yR$ with $x,y\ge0$, so the cube can be dissected into $n=1+m$ cubes for every
$$n\ge N(d):=1+P(R-1).$$
All pieces are smaller than the unit cube because $n\ge2$. (For $d=2$: $P=3$, $R=8$, so every $n\ge22$ works; in fact every $n\ge6$ is possible for the square.) ∎

imc-2000-08.title: Minimum on a well-chosen subinterval
imc-2000-08.body:
Let $(u,v)\subseteq[0,1]$ be a non-empty open interval. Choose $u<\alpha<c<\beta<v$.

Since $f$ is not monotone on $[\alpha,c]$, it is in particular not non-decreasing there: there are $\alpha\le p<q\le c$ with $f(p)>f(q)$. Since $f$ is not non-increasing on $[c,\beta]$, there are $c\le r<s\le\beta$ with $f(r)<f(s)$.

By the extreme value theorem the continuous function $f$ attains its minimum on $[p,s]$ at some point $t$. Because $q,r\in[p,s]$,
$$f(t)\le f(q)<f(p)\quad\text{and}\quad f(t)\le f(r)<f(s),$$
so $t\ne p$ and $t\ne s$, i.e. $t\in(p,s)$. Then $f(t)\le f(x)$ for all $x$ in the open neighbourhood $(p,s)$ of $t$, so $f$ has a local minimum at $t$, and $t\in(p,s)\subset(u,v)$.

So every non-empty open interval contains a local minimum point: these points are dense. ∎

imc-2000-09.title: Count multiplicities against the roots of $p'$
imc-2000-09.body:
For $n=0$ the statement is false ($p\equiv 5$ takes neither value), so we assume $n\ge1$, as intended.

Let $S_0=\{z:p(z)=0\}$ and $S_1=\{z:p(z)=1\}$; they are disjoint. For a polynomial $h$ and $c\in\mathbb C$ let $\mu(h,c)$ be the multiplicity of $c$ as a root of $h$ ($0$ if $h(c)\ne0$). Since $p$ and $p-1$ both have degree $n$,
$$\sum_{c\in S_0}\mu(p,c)=n,\qquad\sum_{c\in S_1}\mu(p-1,c)=n. \tag{1}$$

If $c$ is a root of $h$ of multiplicity $m\ge1$, then $c$ is a root of $h'$ of multiplicity exactly $m-1$ (write $h=(z-c)^mg$ with $g(c)\ne0$; then $h'=(z-c)^{m-1}(mg+(z-c)g')$ and the second factor is $mg(c)\ne0$ at $c$). Both $p$ and $p-1$ have derivative $p'$, hence
$$\mu(p',c)=\mu(p,c)-1\ (c\in S_0),\qquad \mu(p',c)=\mu(p-1,c)-1\ (c\in S_1).$$
Since $n\ge1$, $p'$ is a non-zero polynomial of degree $n-1$, so the total multiplicity of its roots in $S_0\cup S_1$ is at most $n-1$:
$$n-1\ \ge\sum_{c\in S_0\cup S_1}\mu(p',c)=\sum_{c\in S_0}(\mu(p,c)-1)+\sum_{c\in S_1}(\mu(p-1,c)-1)=2n-|S_0|-|S_1| ,$$
using (1). Hence $|S_0|+|S_1|\ge n+1$: there are at least $n+1$ distinct points where $p$ takes the value $0$ or $1$. ∎

imc-2000-10.title: Factor the difference from the tangent line
imc-2000-10.body:
Let the line be $\ell(x)=mx+t$ and the polynomial $p$, of degree $6$, and let $x_1<x_2<x_3$ be the abscissas of $A_1,A_2,A_3$. Tangency at $A_i$ means $p(x_i)=\ell(x_i)$ and $p'(x_i)=m$, so each $x_i$ is (at least) a double root of the degree-6 polynomial $p-\ell$. Hence
$$p(x)-\ell(x)=c\,(x-x_1)^2(x-x_2)^2(x-x_3)^2,\qquad c\ne0 .$$
This does not change sign, so the figure bounded by the segment $A_iA_{i+1}$ and the graph is the region between the line and the graph over $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$, with area $|c|\int_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}}(x-x_1)^2(x-x_2)^2(x-x_3)^2\,dx$.

Lengths on the line are proportional to horizontal projections: $A_iA_{i+1}=(x_{i+1}-x_i)\sqrt{1+m^2}$. Shift coordinates so that $x_2=0$, and put $x_1=-u$, $x_3=v$ with $u,v>0$; then $k=v/u$.

**a)** If $u=v$, the integrand $x^2(x^2-u^2)^2$ is even, so $\int_{-u}^0=\int_0^u$ and the two areas are equal.

**b)** Direct integration (expand the polynomial, or substitute $x=-us$ resp. $x=vs$) gives
$$\int_{-u}^{0}(x+u)^2x^2(x-v)^2\,dx=\frac{u^7}{210}\,(7k^2+7k+2),\qquad \int_{0}^{v}(x+u)^2x^2(x-v)^2\,dx=\frac{u^7k^5}{210}\,(2k^2+7k+7).$$
To see the first one, substitute $x=-us$ ($0\le s\le1$): then $x+u=u(1-s)$, $x=-us$, $x-v=-u(s+k)$, and
$$\int_{-u}^{0}(x+u)^2x^2(x-v)^2\,dx=u^7\int_0^1 s^2(1-s)^2(s^2+2ks+k^2)\,ds .$$
With $\int_0^1 s^a(1-s)^b\,ds=\frac{a!\,b!}{(a+b+1)!}$ the three pieces are $\frac{4!\,2!}{7!}=\frac1{105}$, $2k\cdot\frac{3!\,2!}{6!}=\frac{k}{30}$ and $k^2\cdot\frac{2!\,2!}{5!}=\frac{k^2}{30}$, which add up to $\frac{2+7k+7k^2}{210}$. The second integral is the first one with the roles of $u$ and $v$ exchanged (substitute $x\mapsto-x$): it equals $\frac{v^7}{210}\bigl(7\frac{u^2}{v^2}+7\frac uv+2\bigr)=\frac{u^7k^5}{210}(2k^2+7k+7)$.

Hence the ratio of the area over $[x_2,x_3]$ to the area over $[x_1,x_2]$ is
$$K=k^5\cdot\frac{2k^2+7k+7}{7k^2+7k+2}.$$
For $k>0$:
$$7(2k^2+7k+7)-2(7k^2+7k+2)=35k+45>0,\qquad 7(7k^2+7k+2)-2(2k^2+7k+7)=45k^2+35k>0,$$
so $\frac27<\frac{2k^2+7k+7}{7k^2+7k+2}<\frac72$, and multiplying by $k^5>0$ gives $\frac27k^5<K<\frac72k^5$. ∎

imc-2000-11.title: Show $f\le1$, then use injectivity
imc-2000-11.body:
**Step 1: $f\le1$ and $f$ is non-increasing.** Suppose $f(x)>1$ for some $x$. Put $y=\frac{x}{f(x)-1}>0$; then $yf(x)=x+y$, and the equation gives $f(x)f(x+y)=f(x+y)$, so $f(x)=1$, a contradiction. Hence $f(x)\le1$ for all $x$, and then $f(x+y)=f(x)f(yf(x))\le f(x)$: $f$ is non-increasing.

**Step 2: if $f(x_0)=1$ for some $x_0$, then $f\equiv1$.** With $x=x_0$ the equation reads $f(y)=f(x_0+y)$ for all $y>0$. Given $y$ and $t>0$ choose $n$ with $nx_0\ge t$; then $f(y)=f(y+nx_0)\le f(y+t)\le f(y)$. So $f$ is constant, $f\equiv c$, and $c^2=c$ gives $c=1$.

**Step 3: if $f<1$ everywhere.** Then $f(x+y)=f(x)\,f(yf(x))<f(x)$, so $f$ is strictly decreasing and in particular injective. Fix $x,y>0$ and write $u=yf(x)$ and $w=x+y(1-f(x))>0$, so that $u+w=x+y$. Applying the equation twice,
$$f(x)f(u)=f(x+y)=f(u+w)=f(u)\,f\bigl(wf(u)\bigr).$$
Cancelling $f(u)>0$ and using injectivity: $x=wf(u)$, i.e.
$$x=\bigl(x+y(1-f(x))\bigr)\,f\bigl(yf(x)\bigr).$$
Take $x=1$ and let $c=f(1)\in(0,1)$. For any $z>0$ put $y=z/c$: then $1=\bigl(1+\tfrac zc(1-c)\bigr)f(z)$, so
$$f(z)=\frac{1}{1+az},\qquad a=\frac{1-c}{c}>0 .$$

**Check.** For $f(x)=\frac1{1+ax}$ with $a\ge0$ (Step 2 is the case $a=0$):
$$f(x)f(yf(x))=\frac{1}{1+ax}\cdot\frac{1}{1+\frac{ay}{1+ax}}=\frac{1}{1+ax+ay}=f(x+y).$$

**Answer:** $f(x)=\dfrac1{1+ax}$ for a constant $a\ge0$. ∎

imc-2000-12.title: Eigenvalues: $AB$ and $BA$ have the same characteristic polynomial
imc-2000-12.body:
The statement is **true**.

**Fact 1.** For square matrices $X,Y$ of the same size, $XY$ and $YX$ have the same characteristic polynomial. Indeed, with $P=\begin{pmatrix}I&X\\0&I\end{pmatrix}$,
$$P^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}XY&0\\Y&0\end{pmatrix}P=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\Y&YX\end{pmatrix},$$
so $t^m\chi_{XY}(t)=t^m\chi_{YX}(t)$, hence $\chi_{XY}=\chi_{YX}$.

**Fact 2.** If $M$ is a complex $m\times m$ matrix with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m$ (with multiplicity), then $p(e^M)$ has eigenvalues $p(e^{\lambda_1}),\dots,p(e^{\lambda_m})$. Indeed, write $M=UTU^{-1}$ with $T$ upper triangular with diagonal $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m$ (Schur/Jordan triangularization over $\mathbb C$). Powers of $T$ are upper triangular with diagonal $\lambda_i^n$, so $e^M=Ue^TU^{-1}$ with $e^T$ upper triangular with diagonal $e^{\lambda_i}$, and then $p(e^M)=U\,p(e^T)\,U^{-1}$ with $p(e^T)$ upper triangular with diagonal $p(e^{\lambda_i})$.

**Fact 3.** A matrix is nilpotent iff all its eigenvalues are $0$ (if all eigenvalues are $0$, the characteristic polynomial is $t^m$ and Cayley–Hamilton gives $N^m=0$; conversely $Nv=\lambda v$, $N^k=0$ give $\lambda^k=0$).

Now by Fact 1, $AB$ and $BA$ have the same eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m$. By Facts 2 and 3,
$$p(e^{AB})\text{ nilpotent}\iff p(e^{\lambda_i})=0\ \forall i\iff p(e^{BA})\text{ nilpotent}.$$
**Answer: True.** ∎

imc-2000-12.title: Write $q(e^{AB})=c_0I+AC$ and $q(e^{BA})=c_0I+CA$
imc-2000-12.body:
For a polynomial $q$, expanding $q(e^X)$ gives a convergent power series $q(e^X)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_nX^n$ with real coefficients $c_n$ depending only on $q$. Put
$$C=\sum_{n\ge1}c_n\,B(AB)^{n-1}=\sum_{n\ge1}c_n(BA)^{n-1}B .$$
Then $q(e^{AB})=c_0I+AC$ and $q(e^{BA})=c_0I+CA$. Since $AC$ and $CA$ have the same characteristic polynomial $g(t)$ (Fact 1 of the first solution), both $q(e^{AB})$ and $q(e^{BA})$ have characteristic polynomial $g(t-c_0)$.

Suppose $p(e^{AB})^k=0$ and take $q=p^k$. Then $q(e^{AB})=0$ has characteristic polynomial $t^m$, so the same holds for $q(e^{BA})=p(e^{BA})^k$; by Cayley–Hamilton $\bigl(p(e^{BA})^k\bigr)^m=0$, i.e. $p(e^{BA})$ is nilpotent. The converse follows by swapping $A$ and $B$. **Answer: True.** ∎
